title: Isaiah 33:1–16
context: Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed; O LORD, be gracious to us; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness; who among us can dwell with the consuming fire; he who walks righteously. The unit stays with historic Assyria over Isaiah’s Judah—Sennacherib the spoiler, the broken covenant, Hezekiah’s times, Zion’s sinners afraid—as Wesley and Calvin actually read—not a newspaper of later destroyers.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on the destroyer not yet destroyed, the LORD gracious, Zion filled with justice, who can dwell with consuming fire, and he who walks righteously—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 33:1–16.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: To thee—Sennacherib, who wasted the land of Judah. O Lord—the prophet contemplating the judgment which was now coming upon God’s people, directs his prayer to God for them. Their arm—our arm or strength. The change of persons is frequent in prophetical writings. Every morning—when we offer the morning sacrifice, and call upon thee; the sense is, help us speedily and continually. The noise—which the angel shall make in destroying the army. The people—those of the army, who escaped that stroke. Your spoil—that treasure which you have raked together, by spoiling divers people. Gathered—by the Jews at Jerusalem, when you flee away. Exalted—by the destruction of so potent an army, and by the defense of this people. Thy times—he turns his speech to Hezekiah. Thy throne shall be established upon the sure foundations of wisdom and justice. The fear—thy chief treasure is in promoting the fear and worship of God. The ambassadors—whom he shall send to beg peace of the Assyrian. Shall weep—because they cannot obtain their desires. The covenant—Sennacherib broke his faith, given to Hezekiah, of departing for a sum of money. Cities—the defensed cities of Judah, which he contemned, and easily took. Mourneth—being desolate and neglected. Hewn—by the Assyrians. Stubble—instead of solid corn. Your great hopes and designs shall be utterly disappointed. Your breath—your rage against my people shall bring ruin upon yourselves. The people—shall be burnt as easily and effectually as chalk is burned to lime. The sinners—this is spoken of the Jews. The prophet, having foretold the deliverance of God’s people and the destruction of their enemies, gives a lively representation of the unbelieving condition in which the Jews were, before their deliverance came. Who—how shall we be able to endure, or avoid the wrath of that God, who is a consuming fire; who is now about to destroy us utterly by the Assyrians, and will afterwards burn us with unquenchable fire? He—who is just in all his dealings. From hearing—who will not hearken to any counsels, tending to shed innocent blood. From seeing—that abhors the very sight of sin committed by others, and guards his eyes from beholding occasions of sin. On high—out of the reach of danger. His waters—God will furnish him with all necessaries.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 33:1–16)

reformed.quote: Wo to thee that spoilest. It is almost universally agreed that this is addressed to Sennacherib and his army; I am not unwilling to believe that the Prophet pronounces against the Assyrians a threatening intended to alleviate the distresses of the people. There will be a wonderful revolution of affairs, which will overthrow Nineveh; the Babylonians will come to punish them for that cruelty which they exercised on other nations. When thou shalt have ceased to plunder: tyrants have boundaries assigned to them which they cannot pass. O Jehovah, have pity upon us: he reminds the godly where they ought to go amidst such distresses—to prayer. Faith alone is the mother of calling on God. Be what thou hast been, their arm in the morning: ancient benefits bestowed by God on the fathers. At the voice of the tumult the peoples fled: their army had been collected out of various nations. I willingly interpret the word voice to mean the loud noise which would be raised by the Medes and Persians. And your prey shall be gathered: most commentators refer it to Sennacherib’s defeat, but that appears to me too limited; the wealth of Nineveh, amassed by robbery, shall be carried to Babylon. Jehovah is exalted, who dwelleth on high: he hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. The stability of thy times: he promises that the state of the kingdom under Hezekiah will yet be happy; these words must be referred to Christ, in whom is found true wisdom and knowledge. The fear of Jehovah is his treasure. The ambassadors of peace wept bitterly: Sennacherib has haughtily refused to make peace. He hath broken the covenant: the cruelty of Sennacherib, treacherously breaking the treaty which he had made with Hezekiah. Now will I rise: the time when the Church appeared to be utterly ruined. Ye shall conceive chaff: the fire kindled by your breath shall devour you. The sinners in Zion are afraid: they who shelter themselves under the name of God. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? God is called a devouring fire; the inward anguish by which ungodly men are tormented, the stings of conscience. He that walketh in righteousness: God is always gracious to his worshippers; this ought to be observed in opposition to the Popish doctors, by whom passages which recommend works are abused in order to destroy the righteousness of faith. He shall dwell in high places: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure.

verses.text: Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed! When you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betraying, they will betray you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: to thee—Sennacherib, who wasted the land of Judah. The woe is still that king’s, who spoiled Judah and had not yet been spoiled.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have ceased to destroy. Historic Sennacherib is already named. The church is not to hunt another destroyer to make “you will be destroyed” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: it is almost universally agreed that this is the beginning of a new discourse, addressed to Sennacherib and his army; he is not unwilling to believe that the Prophet pronounces against the Assyrians a threatening intended to alleviate the distresses of the people. There will be a wonderful revolution which will overthrow Nineveh; the Babylonians will come to punish them for the cruelty they exercised on other nations. When thou shalt have ceased to plunder: tyrants have boundaries assigned to them which they cannot pass.

Reformed accent: the spoiler is still that Assyrian, then Nineveh’s fall to Babylon. The woe stays with Isaiah’s Judah, not a newspaper pasted onto “destroyer.”
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the destroyer as the historic oppressor of Judah, not a newspaper. Wesley names him Sennacherib, who wasted the land of Judah. Calvin is not unwilling to address Sennacherib and his army, yet will not stop the woe there: Nineveh will be plundered by the Babylonians for the cruelty she used on other nations, and Babylon in her turn will be robbed. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.

verses.text: O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: O Lord—the prophet contemplating the judgment which was now coming upon God’s people, directs his prayer to God for them. Their arm—our arm or strength. The change of persons is frequent in prophetical writings. Every morning—when we offer the morning sacrifice, and call upon thee; which yet is not meant exclusively, as if he did not desire God’s help at other times, but comprehensively, the morning being put for the whole day. The sense is, help us speedily and continually.

Arminian reading: they might yet have waited and been helped. The prayer is still Isaiah’s over that coming stroke. The church is not to stretch “every morning” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: this sentiment was added in order to remind the godly where they ought to go amidst such distresses—to prayer, to supplicate from God the fulfillment of these promises. Faith alone is the mother of calling on God. Be what thou hast been, their arm in the morning: he supplies “who hast been,” in order to bring forward the ancient benefits bestowed by God on the fathers. Arm denotes the power exerted in defense of his Church before she was afflicted; salvation denotes the deliverance by which he rescues her even when she appears to be ruined.

Reformed note: the arm is still the Lord’s over that people in trouble. The graciousness stays with Isaiah’s wait, not a newspaper of later mornings.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the prayer as Isaiah’s over that Assyrian distress, not a newspaper. Wesley reads “their arm” as a change of persons for our arm, and “every morning” as the morning sacrifice—help speedily and continually. Calvin reads “their arm in the morning” by supplying “who hast been”: ancient benefits to the fathers, so faith waits on the God who already delivered them. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.

verses.text: At the tumultuous noise peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, nations are scattered,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the noise—which the angel shall make in destroying the army. The people—those of the army, who escaped that stroke. The nations—the people of divers nations, which made up this army. The tumult is still the angel’s over Sennacherib’s host after the prayer of v. 2.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have fled at that noise. Historic Assyria’s mixed army is already named. The church is not to hunt another tumult to make “peoples flee” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he makes use of the plural number, saying that they were peoples; for the kingdom of the Assyrians consisted of various peoples, and their army had been collected out of various nations. At thy exaltation: the Lord, who formerly seemed as it were to remain at rest, now suddenly came forth to public view. He willingly interprets the word voice to mean the loud noise which would be raised by the Medes and Persians.

Reformed accent: the scattering is still that empire’s. The lift stays with the Lord’s coming forth over Assyria, not a newspaper pasted onto “nations are scattered.”

verses.text: and your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leapt upon.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: your spoil—that treasure which you have raked together, by spoiling divers people. Gathered—by the Jews at Jerusalem, when you flee away. Like the caterpillar—as caterpillars gather and devour the fruits of the earth. As locusts—as locusts, especially when they are armed by commission from God, come with great force, and run hither and thither.

Arminian reading: they might yet have gathered what the spoiler dropped in flight. The leap is still Jerusalem’s over that army’s hoard. The church is not to stretch “caterpillar” into a later raid.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he addresses the Assyrians. The latter opinion—Sennacherib’s defeat before Jerusalem—has been adopted by almost all commentators, but it appears to him too limited; the Prophet intended to express something more, the destruction of that nation. He compares that warlike nation to caterpillars, because they will have no power to resist, and shall be gathered into heaps to be destroyed. According to the running of locusts: the Babylonians will run like locusts to devour the whole country; the wealth of Nineveh, amassed by robbery, shall be carried to Babylon.

Reformed note: the prey is still Assyria’s. The gathering stays with that monarchy’s fall, not a newspaper of later spoils.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the spoil as that army’s plunder in the Assyrian crisis, not a newspaper. Wesley reads the gathering as the Jews at Jerusalem taking what the spoiler raked together, when the army flees. Calvin thinks the Sennacherib-defeat reading too limited: caterpillars easily shaken off, locusts the Babylonians running over the land, Nineveh’s wealth carried to Babylon. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.

verses.text: The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: exalted—by the destruction of so potent an army, and by the defense of this people. The filling of Zion is still after that army’s fall, historic Judah’s Zion.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have seen Zion filled. The Lord’s high dwelling is already enough. The church is not to hunt another mountain to make “justice and righteousness” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: Jehovah is exalted, who dwelleth on high. Wicked men imagine that he was cast down by the destruction of the people; he inhabiteth the heavens. He hath filled Zion with judgment and righteousness: a proof of God’s wonderful kindness when the Jews shall be delivered; the fullness of righteousness and judgment means that God will largely pour forth his kindness in restoring the Church. Holy and well-adjusted order, not corruptible riches, is the standard by which prosperity should be judged.

Reformed accent: Zion is still that restored city. The filling stays with the Lord’s high seat over her, not a newspaper pasted onto “justice.”

verses.text: and he will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion’s treasure.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: thy times—he turns his speech to Hezekiah. Thy throne shall be established upon the sure foundations of wisdom and justice. And strength—thy strong salvation. The fear—thy chief treasure is in promoting the fear and worship of God. The times are still that king’s after Zion is filled in v. 5.

Arminian reading: they might yet have had that throne established. Historic Hezekiah is already named. Wesley’s own later note on the king of v. 17 will add Christ; this verse’s treasure is not a millennial chart and not a newspaper of later courts.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he promises that the state of the kingdom under the reign of Hezekiah will yet be happy and prosperous, especially when he contrasts it with the ruinous aspect it exhibited under Ahaz. Since the kingdom of Hezekiah was but a slender shadow of the kingdom of Christ, these words must be referred to Christ, in whom is found true wisdom and knowledge. The fear of Jehovah is his treasure, the teacher of piety, not cold or lifeless.

Reformed note: Calvin and Wesley both keep Hezekiah’s times in that Judah; Calvin adds the reference to Christ as end. This stability is already enough without a later newspaper. No millennial dispute is in this comment.

verses.text: Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: behold—that the mercy promised might be duly magnified, he makes a lively representation of their great danger and distress. The ambassadors—whom he shall send to beg peace of the Assyrian. Shall weep—because they cannot obtain their desires. The weeping is still Hezekiah’s embassy after the treasure of v. 6.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have obtained peace and did not. Historic Assyria is already named. The church is not to hunt another street to make “weep bitterly” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the ambassadors of peace wept bitterly. It is given as a token of despair, that the ambassadors who had been sent to appease the tyrant were unsuccessful; every way of obtaining peace was attempted by Hezekiah, without any success. Sennacherib has haughtily and disdainfully refused to make peace, so that the ambassadors are constrained to pour out in public their grief.

Reformed accent: the envoys are still that court’s. The bitter weeping stays with the refused treaty, not a newspaper of later talks.

verses.text: The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the covenant—Sennacherib broke his faith, given to Hezekiah, of departing for a sum of money, 2 Kings 18:14, 17. Cities—the defensed cities of Judah, which he contemned, and easily took. The waste is still that invasion’s, after the weeping envoys of v. 7.

Arminian reading: they might yet have kept the paid-for peace. Historic 2 Kings 18 is already named. The church is not to stretch “covenants are broken” into a later map.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the roads are deserted, so that no one shall go in or out, which commonly happens when war has been declared. He hath broken the covenant: this is part of the description of the cruelty and insatiable rage of Sennacherib, in treacherously breaking the treaty which he had formerly made with Hezekiah; as soon as an opportunity presented itself for invading Judea, he violated his promise. He hath despised the cities; he hath regarded no man.

Reformed note: Calvin refuses to read this as a complaint that God does not fulfill his promises. The broken faith stays with that Assyrian, not a newspaper pasted onto “highways.”

verses.text: The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: mourneth—being desolate and neglected. Hewn—by the Assyrians. Bashan—two places eminent for fertility, are spoiled of their fruits. Lebanon, Sharon, Bashan, and Carmel are still that land’s after the broken covenant of v. 8.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have seen the fertile places stripped. Historic Assyria’s hewing is already named. The church is not to hunt another Lebanon to make “the land mourns” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he describes more fully how wretched and desperate the Jews would perceive their condition to be. The places specified—Lebanon, Bashan, and Carmel—are widely distant from each other and form almost the farthest boundaries of the holy land, in order to shew that no part of it will remain safe. To Lebanon he assigns confusion, because it is elsewhere mentioned as beautiful; Sharon, a fertile district, will be like a wilderness; Bashan and Carmel, which abounded in fruits, will be shaken.

Reformed accent: the mourning is still the holy land’s under that invasion. The leaves stay with those named ridges, not a newspaper of later deserts.

verses.text: “Now I will arise,” says the LORD, “now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley does not gloss this verse. His notes run from Bashan and Carmel spoiled in v. 9 to the stubble of v. 11. The “now” is still the LORD’s rise over that same Assyrian wasting of the land—historic Judah first.

Arminian close of the wait: they might yet have seen him arise. Wesley and Calvin both keep this rise as the Lord’s over that crisis; this is not an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight. The church is not to stretch “now I will arise” into a later newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: now will I rise. There is great force in the particle now, and in the repetition, I shall be exalted, I shall be lifted up on high. We ought to observe the time to which these statements relate, that is, when the Church appeared to be utterly ruined; God declares that he will judge that to be the most suitable time for rendering assistance. He thus delays to render assistance because it is useful to exercise the patience of the godly, to try their faith, to subdue the desires of the flesh, to excite to earnestness in prayer; therefore he lays a restraint, that they may not with headlong eagerness anticipate that period which God has already marked out for them.

Reformed note: the marked period is still that ruin under Assyria. The rise stays with the Lord’s own hour, not a newspaper pasted onto “now.”

verses.text: You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble; your breath is a fire that will consume you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: stubble—instead of solid corn. Your great hopes and designs shall be utterly disappointed. Your breath—your rage against my people shall bring ruin upon yourselves. The chaff is still that spoiler’s after the LORD arises in v. 10.

Arminian reading: they might yet have conceived something other than chaff. Historic rage against Judah is already named. The church is not to hunt another breath to make “consume you” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: ye shall conceive chaff. He now addresses the enemies of the Church; their insolence is foolish and to no purpose. It is customary to employ conceptions for the designs and efforts of men; their conception shall be fruitless. The fire of your breath shall devour you: the fire kindled by your breath shall devour you. We commonly kindle a fire by blowing; the fire which wicked men have blown by their wicked contrivances shall be destructive to them. Let us learn that what Isaiah foretold about Sennacherib relates to all the adversaries of believers and of the Church.

Reformed accent: the stubble is still that army’s hope. The fire stays with their own breath against Judah, not a newspaper of later plots.

verses.text: And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the people—shall be burnt as easily and effectually as chalk is burned to lime. The burning is still that host’s after the chaff of v. 11.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have been lime in a moment. Historic Assyria’s peoples are already named. The church is not to stretch “thorns cut down” into a later pyre.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the peoples shall be the burnings of lime. He compares them to the burning of lime, because their hardness shall be bruised, as fire softens the stones, so that they shall easily be reduced to powder. As thorns cut up: there is no kind of wood that burns more violently or is more quickly consumed. We know that this was fulfilled in Sennacherib, for the event proved the truth of these predictions, though they appeared to be altogether incredible.

Reformed note: the lime is still that army’s. The thorns stay with Sennacherib’s host, not a newspaper pasted onto “burned in the fire.”

verses.text: Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley does not gloss this verse. His notes run from the people burnt to lime in v. 12 to the sinners in Zion in v. 14. The hearing is still of what the Lord has done in that Assyrian burning—far and near over historic Judah.

Arminian close of the lime: they might yet have acknowledged that might. Wesley and Calvin both keep the deed as the Lord’s against that host; this is not an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight. The church is not to hunt another far-off people to make “acknowledge my might” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: hear, ye that are far off. Isaiah here makes a preface, as if he were about to speak on a very weighty subject; he bids his hearers be attentive. He addresses both those who are near, who would be eyewitnesses of this event, and the most distant nations to whom the report would be communicated. The power of God will be such as to be perceived not only by a few persons, or by those who are at hand, but also by those at a very great distance. It will be a striking and extraordinary demonstration of the power of God.

Reformed accent: far and near still hear that deed over Assyria. The might stays with what he has done, not a newspaper of later acknowledgments.

verses.text: The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: “Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the sinners—this is spoken of the Jews. The prophet, having foretold the deliverance of God’s people and the destruction of their enemies, gives a lively representation of the unbelieving condition in which the Jews were, before their deliverance came. Who—how shall we be able to endure, or avoid the wrath of that God, who is a consuming fire; who is now about to destroy us utterly by the Assyrians, and will afterwards burn us with unquenchable fire?

Arminian reading: they might yet have feared before the stroke. Historic Zion’s unbelievers are already named. The church is not to stretch “consuming fire” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the sinners in Zion are afraid. When he employs the word Zion, he reproves the degenerate Jews, because, covered with the shadow of the sanctuary, they thought they possessed a fortress which could not be stormed; the haughtiest of all men are they who shelter themselves under the name of God. Terror hath seized the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? Some view the words as relating to the king of Assyria; he prefers the latter opinion, God. God is called a devouring fire; the inward anguish by which ungodly men are tormented, the stings of conscience which cannot be allayed, the unquenchable burning of crimes. God is usually kind and gentle to the godly, while wicked men feel that he is severe and terrible.

Reformed accent: the fire is still the Lord’s over Zion’s hypocrites in that hour. The trembling stays with those sinners, not a newspaper pasted onto “everlasting burnings.”
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the sinners as Zion’s own, afraid in that historic hour, not a newspaper. Wesley reads their cry as the Jews’ unbelief before deliverance: God a consuming fire, about to destroy them by the Assyrians, and afterwards to burn them with unquenchable fire. Calvin will not make the fire chiefly the king of Assyria: God himself is the devouring fire; hypocrites who sheltered under his name feel inward anguish and the stings of conscience. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.

verses.text: He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: he—who is just in all his dealings. From hearing—who will not hearken to any counsels, tending to shed innocent blood. From seeing—that abhors the very sight of sin committed by others, and guards his eyes from beholding occasions of sin. The walker is still the answer to Zion’s cry in v. 14.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have walked this way. Historic Zion’s just man is already enough. The church is not to hunt another pair of hands to make “walks righteously” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he that walketh in righteousness. He convinces them of their guilt and exhorts them to repentance; there is a state of friendship between God and men if they wish to follow and practice righteousness, maintain truth and integrity, and act inoffensively towards their neighbors. He treats of the second table of the Law, by which the sincerity of godliness is put to the test. This discourse is directed chiefly against hypocrites, who throw a false veil of piety over their hidden pollutions. Who speaketh what is right; who despiseth the gain arising from violence; who shaketh his hands from accepting a bribe; who stoppeth his ear that it may not hear blood; who shutteth his eyes from seeing evil.

Reformed note: the walk is still that man’s in Zion. The shut eyes stay with Isaiah’s answer to the fire, not a newspaper of later virtue.

verses.text: he will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: on high—out of the reach of danger. His waters—God will furnish him with all necessaries. The heights are still that just man’s after the walk of v. 15, historic Zion under Assyria.

Arminian close of the unit: they might yet have dwelt out of reach. Wesley’s necessaries are already the Lord’s gift in that siege, not a later chart. The church is not to stretch “water will be sure” into a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he shall dwell in high places. They who were described in the former verse are not subject to that burning; they shall be made to dwell in a place of the greatest safety, a habitation among fortified rocks. Bread shall be given to him; his waters shall be sure: to a safe dwelling he adds an abundance of good things. No man can be so holy or upright as to be capable of enduring the eye of God; we therefore need a mediator, through whose intercession our sins may be forgiven. The Prophet did not intend to set aside the ordinary doctrine of Scripture on this subject; this ought to be carefully observed in opposition to the Popish doctors, by whom passages of this kind, which recommend works, are abused in order to destroy the righteousness of faith.

Reformed close: the rocks are still that Zion’s. Calvin and Wesley agree the dweller is kept in the Assyrian hour; Calvin will not let the walk become a ladder against faith. This defense is already enough without a later newspaper.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the dweller as the righteous man kept in that Zion, not a newspaper. Wesley reads the heights as out of the reach of danger, and the waters as God furnishing all necessaries. Calvin reads the same munitions and sure bread, yet will not let the walk of v. 15 become a Popish ladder against the righteousness of faith: no man is so holy as to endure the eye of God without a mediator. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.
